title: COA chair hurdles CA confirmation
summary: Commission on Audit Chairman Douglas Michael Mallillin received the nod of the Commission on Appointments yesterday despite an initial protest from one of the senators.

blocks.text: Senators and Commission on Appointments officials have a group photo at the Senate yesterday with generals and flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

MANILA, Philippines — Commission on Audit (COA) Chairman Douglas Michael Mallillin received the nod of the Commission on Appointments (CA) yesterday despite an initial protest from one of the senators.

Before he received his confirmation from the CA committee and in plenary, President Marcos’ sister-turned-critic Sen. Imee Marcos grilled Mallillin about possible conflicts of interest in his work as the country’s auditor, noting his extensive experience with private firms.

She also flagged the COA’s role in helping the administration investigate the opposition, in an apparent reference to the disallowance of Vice President Sara Duterte’s confidential funds, an impeachment article that was later withdrawn by the House prosecution panel.
“Serious concerns have arisen over the manner by which the Commission on Audit has exercised its powers against members of the political opposition, both local and national,” Marcos said.

“I speak for many of these government officials, both elected and appointed, who are now worried that the COA, rather than serving exclusively as an impartial guardian of public funds, has been allowed to become an instrument of political harassment in certain cases, with its wide-ranging and considerable investigative and auditing powers being directed against those who dare to oppose the administration,” she added.
Asked to respond, Mallillin denied having any conflict of interest in his stint as COA commissioner before being appointed to replace Gamaliel Cordoba, who was named Supreme Court Associate Justice.
Mallillin’s term will only be until February 2029, serving Cordoba’s remaining term.
Mallillin vowed to “commit to be an independent commission as mandated by our Constitution without fear or favor” in response to Marcos’ claim of allowing the COA to be used for political harassment.

When asked by Sen. Risa Hontiveros what the COA intends to do with its confidential funds audit, Mallillin said the agency under his helm would “protect the identity of the people who are the informants and recipients of the funds, but without circumventing the internal controls that should be present in issuing confidential fund.”
Marcos later withdrew her opposition after colleagues put her protest to a vote, paving the way for Mallillin’s nomination to be approved and endorsed to plenary for final approval.

Sens. Joel Villanueva and Raffy Tulfo voted for Mallillin’s nomination in plenary, citing his experience as both lawyer and accountant and in having strict audit requirements, such as geotagging coordinates to prevent ghost projects.
Besides him, the CA confirmed the ad interim appointments and nominations of 15 generals and flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines yesterday.
The CA also welcomed former Senate secretary Mark Llandro Mendoza as the CA’s new secretary.
